---
title: "Offline-first rendering & theming"
---

Three subsystems, math, syntax highlighting, and theming, look unrelated but
follow one principle: **render server-side, ship offline, and emit theme-agnostic
output so a light/dark toggle restyles the page with nothing to re-render.** It is
worth stating on its own because it shapes how each of them is built.

## Render in Rust, ship offline

Our `post.qmd` carries both kinds of content the browser should never have to
render for itself, the `$T(t) = …$` math and the Python block. Both are handled at
render time, in Rust, not by a client-side pass:

- **Math** (`math.rs`) runs KaTeX in an embedded JS engine and emits static
  HTML + MathML at parse time. The only client dependency is KaTeX's stylesheet, whose
  woff2 fonts are inlined into it as `data:` URIs at build time (`build.rs`), so even the
  math fonts need no network. A static build ships that stylesheet **only on pages that
  actually contain math**; the live preview always carries it, since any edit can add an
  equation.
- **Highlighting** (`highlight.rs`) colours code with `syntect`, in Rust, rather
  than shipping highlight.js. It aliases common language tokens (`js`/`ojs` → javascript,
  `py` → python, `rs` → rust) and falls back to plain escaped text for an unrecognized
  language, so a fenced block always renders.

The payoff is the same in both cases, and it is why they are built this way:

1. the exported HTML is **self-contained**, no CDN for a built post's own math or
   highlighting;
2. the **first paint is already correct**, no flash of plain code or unrendered
   `$…$` while a client script boots, and nothing to re-run after each block
   update;
3. the work lives in the **corpus-tested Rust half**, not in untested browser JS.

## Theme-agnostic output

The second half of the principle is that none of this output bakes in colours.
Highlighting emits `syntect`'s **scope classes** (each prefixed `qhl-`) rather than
inline colours, and a stylesheet maps those classes to a palette with a
`[data-theme=dark]` override. The same idea runs through the whole page: the
navbar, callouts, figures, and code all read `--qmd-*` CSS custom properties, and a
*theme* is just a `:root` block that sets those variables (a built-in `light`/`dark`
pair, a `.css`/`.scss` file, or an installed `_extensions/<name>/theme.css`, all
resolved in `theme.rs`).

So **a light/dark toggle swaps CSS-variable values and re-styles everything with
nothing to re-render**, no re-highlight, no re-render of math. That is only possible
because the rendered output was theme-agnostic to begin with.

## Memoizing the per-render cost

Rendering server-side has one cost: the dev server re-renders the *whole* document
on every save, and each KaTeX expression is a JS evaluation (roughly a millisecond
each). A math-heavy page would re-render hundreds of expressions on each keystroke,
which adds up to hundreds of milliseconds of work to redraw math that didn't change.
KaTeX output is a pure function of `(latex, display_mode)` under fixed options, so
`math.rs` **memoizes** results in a process-global `HashMap<(String, bool), String>`.
The key is `(latex, display_mode)`: the same expression rendered inline and in display
mode are two distinct entries, so they never alias. After the first render, all the
unchanged math on a save (everything but the block being edited) is a hashmap hit, the
cache persists for the life of the process, and it is shared across a whole site's pages.

The cache is **bounded at 8192 entries**, and clears *wholesale* on overflow rather than
evicting one entry at a time. A real document has a small, stable set of expressions that
a long session never outgrows, so the cap is rarely reached, and when it is, a plain
clear-and-refill is enough: a full LRU isn't worth the complexity for this access pattern.
This is the render-time analogue of [the block diff](block-model.qmd): do the expensive
work once, reuse it everywhere it didn't change.

The memo is transparent: it never changes *what* gets rendered. An expression KaTeX
can't parse is still rendered inline in red (`throw_on_error` is off), and an
engine-level failure still falls back to the escaped source in a `qmd-math-error` span.
The cache only ever skips repeating work whose answer it already has.

## No flash: the pre-paint script

A theme that is chosen at runtime risks a flash of the wrong one. `theme.rs` ships
a small **pre-paint `<head>` script** that runs before the body renders. It:

- sets `<html data-theme>` from the saved choice (`localStorage` key `qmd-theme`),
  else a front-matter-forced `light`/`dark`, else **follows the OS** `prefers-color-scheme`
  (dark when the OS prefers dark, otherwise falling back to light); an unsaved "auto" page
  also re-applies when the OS theme flips, except for a reader who explicitly toggled; and
- sets the `color-scheme` CSS property and the page `background` **inline on
  `<html>`, in that same pre-paint script**, so the browser's canvas (and its native
  form controls, scrollbars, and `<select>` popups) are the theme colour from the very
  first frame. The background comes from a small fixed map in the script itself
  (`{ dark: #16181d, sepia: #f4ecd8, light: #ffffff }`), not from a stylesheet, so it
  is in effect before any CSS parses.

Without that inline background, the canvas stays white until the inline `<style>`
parses, which shows as a white flash on every cross-page navigation in dark mode.
Setting `color-scheme` alongside it is what stops the browser from drawing a *light*
default scrollbar and form-control chrome over a dark page for that same first frame.
The script is shipped *in the page* (not in the preview client) so the toggle and
the no-flash behaviour work in static `build` output too, and it defines the
`qmdSetTheme` / `qmdWireThemeToggles` helpers the navbar and dev-menu toggles call.

## Reader preferences: the same pre-paint trick, applied to typography

Theme is not the only thing a reader gets to choose. The reader menu (the
**Display** section, see [The reader experience](../guide/using/reading.html))
also exposes text size, reading width, and line, letter, and word spacing. These ride
the *same* mechanism as the theme: a value persisted in `localStorage` and applied as a
CSS custom property on `<html>` by the pre-paint head script (`applyReader`), so a
returning reader never sees a flash of the default size before their choice takes hold.

Each control writes through one helper, `qmdSetReaderPref(key, value)`, which stores
`localStorage["qmd-reader-<key>"]` (or removes it when the value is `null`, i.e. the
default) and re-applies. The pre-paint script reads those keys back and sets the matching
variable. The preference lives entirely in the browser: it is per-reader, never written to
the source, and never part of the rendered HTML.

The five knobs, their variables, and their value sets:

| Reader control | localStorage key | CSS variable set | Values (label) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Text size | `qmd-reader-scale` | `--qmd-reader-scale` | `0.9` (small), `1` (normal, default), `1.15` (large), `1.3` (x-large) |
| Reading width | `qmd-reader-width` | `--qmd-maxw` (override) | `38rem` (Narrow), normal (default), `58rem` (Wide) |
| Line spacing | `qmd-reader-leading` | `--qmd-reader-leading` | `1.5` (Tight), `1.7` (Normal, default), `2` (Relaxed) |
| Letter spacing | `qmd-reader-letter` | `--qmd-reader-letter` | `0` (Normal), `0.06em` (Wide), `0.12em` (Wider) |
| Word spacing | `qmd-reader-word` | `--qmd-reader-word` | `0` (Normal), `0.08em` (Wide), `0.16em` (Wider) |

Two details are worth calling out. Width reuses `--qmd-maxw`, the *same* variable the
base theme already uses for the reading column, so a reader's choice is just an override
of that one width, not a separate code path. And the "Wider" letter/word steps are picked
to hit the WCAG 1.4.12 text-spacing minimums (letter `0.12em`, word `0.16em`); the values
are in `em`, so they stay proportional to the reader-scaled font size rather than fighting
it.

::: {.callout-note}
Resetting clears the theme *and* all five reader keys at once (`qmdResetReader`), so a
reader can get back to the document's defaults without clearing site storage by hand.
:::

## The exceptions that must re-render

Theme-agnostic output covers almost everything, but not quite. A few things bake
their colours at render time and a CSS-variable swap can't reach them:

| On a light/dark toggle | What happens |
|---|---|
| Prose, code, callouts, navbar, chrome | CSS variables re-resolve, nothing re-renders |
| KaTeX math | already theme-neutral, untouched |
| Mermaid diagrams | SVG colours are baked at render time, so they **re-render** |
| Theme-matched `{{< video >}}` clips | the now-visible variant is played, the hidden one paused |

The pre-paint script dispatches a `qmd:themechange` event, and exactly those
renderers listen for it. That small, explicit list is the boundary of the
"toggle re-styles with nothing to re-render" rule.
